newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian gold traders eye COMEX short positions.
newsitem.headline: Asian gold traders eye COMEX short positions.

text.p: Gold traders in Hong Kong and Singapore will sit on their hands a while after a non-decision on gold sales from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Wednesday flummoxed the market, industry sources said on Friday.
Hong Kong gold dealers said they would remain cautious as U.S. funds had gone very short in anticipation of IMF gold sales and open interest on COMEX was increasing.
Now the short sellers were left hanging.
"History dictates that the metals are screaming buy when the open interest is rocketing up and the market prices are going down," said one gold trader at an international bank.

Anticipating IMF gold sales, U.S-based investment funds last week began to sell gold short--selling at today's prices gold not yet bought on the basis that prices will drop before delivery has to be made, creating room for profit.

"I'm trying not to take a position either way in gold, but I would play it cautiouly on the short side and be wary as soon as any of the metals show signs of strength," another Hong Kong gold source said.
The shortage of kilobars in the territory will likely be eased by next week, with one gold trader reporting that at least one shipment of gold bars had just arrived at Hong Kong ports.

"Everyone is scrambling to source gold from their suppliers and solve the situation by next week," said a gold dealer at a local bank, adding however that premiums would most likely slip only slightly.
Asian gold prices will continue to drift in a range between $380-$385 an ounce in quiet dealings deadened by a lack of trading interest, Singapore dealers said.
"The focus isn't on bullion, it's on the stock market. It's just treading water," a trader in a European investment house in Singapore said.
"The market is absolutely dead. There's no great shakes to it," another dealer in a Western bank here added.
The IMF's policy-making interim committee may take up the issue of gold sales again at a meeting on Sepember 29, but an agreement at that time seems unlikely, sources said.
Singapore-based dealers expressed growing impatience over the absence of a decision by the Fund.
"They could just keep on delaying that forver," one source said in exasperation.
A decision to sell the gold is expected to drive down prices of the yellow metal, Singapore-based traders said.
"The market's going to struggle. It's really pretty quiet at this point," one dealer said.
With demand barely steady, Singapore gold premiums over spot London prices were quoted unchanged at 35-45 U.S. cents an ounce, dealers said.
